# Part 2: Row-level vs aggregate

#TODO [For each of these three queries, say whether it is row-level or aggregate, and how many rows it returns: (a) `SELECT county FROM covid WHERE state = 'Ohio' AND date = '2020-12-31';` (b) `SELECT max(cases) FROM covid WHERE state = 'Ohio';` (c) `SELECT state, max(cases) FROM covid GROUP BY state;` <2pts>]
(a) Row-level. It returns 88 rows, one for each Ohio county record on December 31, 2020.
(b) Aggregate. It returns 1 row because MAX(cases) computes one maximum across all Ohio records. The maximum is 84,050.
(c) Aggregate. It returns 55 rows. GROUP BY state creates one group for each distinct state value, and MAX(cases) returns one maximum per group.

# Part 4: Computed columns

```sql
#TODO [deaths divided by cases for Cook County, Illinois on 2020-12-31 (with nothing else changed) <1pts>]
SELECT deaths / cases
FROM covid
WHERE county = 'Cook'
  AND state = 'Illinois'
  AND date = '2020-12-31';

-- ?column?
-- 0
```

#TODO [Why did you get 0? <1pts>]
Both deaths and cases are integers, so PostgreSQL uses integer division and drops the fractional part. Since deaths is smaller than cases, the result is 0.

```sql
#TODO [fix the previous query get the actual rate and name the column death_rate <1pts>]
SELECT deaths::numeric / cases AS death_rate
FROM covid
WHERE county = 'Cook'
  AND state = 'Illinois'
  AND date = '2020-12-31';

-- death_rate
-- 0.02104650808328168027
#TODO [the same as a percentage rounded to 2 decimals, named death_rate_pct (you should get 2.10) <1pts>]
SELECT ROUND(100.0 * deaths / cases, 2) AS death_rate_pct
FROM covid
WHERE county = 'Cook'
  AND state = 'Illinois'
  AND date = '2020-12-31';

-- death_rate_pct
-- 2.10
#TODO [on 2020-12-31: the county, state and death_rate_pct of the 5 counties with at least 10000 cases that have the highest death rate (leave out the missing deaths) <2pts>]
SELECT county,
       state,
       ROUND(100.0 * deaths / cases, 2) AS death_rate_pct
FROM covid
WHERE date = '2020-12-31'
  AND cases >= 10000
  AND deaths IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY deaths::numeric / cases DESC
LIMIT 5;

-- county        | state         | death_rate_pct
-- New York City | New York      | 5.84
-- Somerset      | New Jersey    | 5.23
-- Essex         | New Jersey    | 5.04
-- Bergen        | New Jersey    | 4.89
-- Norfolk       | Massachusetts | 4.77
```

# Part 5: `CASE`

```sql
#TODO [on 2020-12-31: label each county 'high' if it has at least 1000 deaths, 'medium' if at least 100 and 'low' otherwise, name the label size, and count the counties in each label <2pts>]
SELECT CASE
           WHEN deaths >= 1000 THEN 'high'
           WHEN deaths >= 100 THEN 'medium'
           ELSE 'low'
       END AS size,
       COUNT(*) AS county_count
FROM covid
WHERE date = '2020-12-31'
GROUP BY size
ORDER BY county_count DESC;

-- size   | county_count
-- low    | 2697
-- medium | 487
-- high   | 61
```

#TODO [78 counties have a missing deaths value on 2020-12-31. Which label did they get, and why? Is that label correct? <1pts>]
All 78 counties received the label 'low'. Comparisons with NULL evaluate to unknown, so neither WHEN condition is true and CASE uses the ELSE branch. A better label would be 'unknown', because the number of deaths is missing.

# Part 7: Missing data helpers: `coalesce` and `NULLIF`

```sql
#TODO [on 2020-12-31, in one query: the number of rows, the number with a recorded deaths value, the mean deaths rounded to 2 decimals, and the mean deaths with the missing values counted as 0, rounded to 2 decimals <2pts>]
SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_rows,
       COUNT(deaths) AS recorded_deaths,
       ROUND(AVG(deaths), 2) AS avg_recorded,
       ROUND(AVG(COALESCE(deaths, 0)), 2) AS avg_missing_as_zero
FROM covid
WHERE date = '2020-12-31';

-- total_rows | recorded_deaths | avg_recorded | avg_missing_as_zero
-- 3245       | 3167            | 109.27       | 106.64
```

#TODO [Which of the two means is the right "average deaths per county", and why? <1pts>]
109.27 is the average for the 3,167 counties with reported deaths. The lower average, 106.64, assumes that all 78 counties with missing values had zero deaths. We cannot determine the average for all counties without knowing those missing values.

```sql
#TODO [on 2020-12-31: the county, state, cases, deaths and death rate (in percent) of every county with 0 cases, without a division-by-zero error <1pts>]
SELECT county,
       state,
       cases,
       deaths,
       100.0 * deaths / NULLIF(cases, 0) AS death_rate_pct
FROM covid
WHERE date = '2020-12-31'
  AND cases = 0
ORDER BY state, county;

-- county  | state    | cases | deaths | death_rate_pct
-- Unknown | Kansas   | 0     | 408    |
-- Unknown | Maryland | 0     | 57     |
```

#TODO [Why do the `SELECT ... LIMIT 5` parts need parentheses around them? <1pts>]
The parentheses make each ORDER BY and LIMIT 5 apply to its own SELECT, so each date contributes its five highest-case counties before the set operation runs. A LIMIT at the end without parentheses applies to the combined result.

```sql
#TODO [a report of the 3 states with the most deaths on 2020-12-31, with one extra row at the bottom 'all states' and the total deaths of the whole country <2pts>]
-- state      | total_deaths
-- New York   | 37557
-- Texas      | 28155
-- California | 25965
-- all states | 346050
```

#TODO [Why `UNION ALL` and not `UNION` for the report above? <1pts>]
UNION ALL appends the summary row to the three state rows without checking for duplicates. UNION would return the same four rows in this report because their state labels are distinct.


Run this query:

```sql
SELECT state, county, count(*)
  FROM covid
  WHERE date = '2020-12-31'
  GROUP BY state;
```

#TODO [Why does it fail? Write a fixed version that counts the counties of each state <2pts>]
The query groups rows by state, but each state can have multiple counties. PostgreSQL cannot return a single county name for a state group. Removing county from SELECT lets COUNT(*) count the county records for each state on that date.

```sql
#TODO [on 2020-12-31: the states with more than 150 counties, and how many each (you should get 2) <1pts>]
SELECT state, COUNT(*) AS county_count
FROM covid
WHERE date = '2020-12-31'
GROUP BY state
HAVING COUNT(*) > 150
ORDER BY county_count DESC;

-- state   | county_count
-- Texas   | 254
-- Georgia | 160
```

#TODO [Why would grouping by `extract(month FROM date)` be wrong if the table had data from both 2020 and 2021, and what does `date_trunc` do differently? <1pts>]
EXTRACT(MONTH FROM date) returns only the month number, so it groups January 2020 and January 2021 together. DATE_TRUNC('month', date) returns the start of the month and preserves the year, so January 2020 and January 2021 go into separate groups.

# Part 11: Indexes

First check that your `lab04` database has no index yet (you made one only in the lecture's `lec04` database):

```sql
\di
```
If you already have an index on `covid`, delete it with `DROP INDEX` and the name that `\di` shows, e.g. for the lecture's index:

```sql
DROP INDEX covid_state_county_idx;
\di
```

Now do these exercises:

```sql
#TODO [run EXPLAIN ANALYZE on the query "the largest cases of Miami-Dade, Florida over the whole year". Write the plan's scan type and the execution time <1pts>]
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT MAX(cases)
FROM covid
WHERE state = 'Florida'
  AND county = 'Miami-Dade';

-- Scan type: Parallel Seq Scan on covid
-- Execution Time: 45.289 ms
#TODO [create an index on (state, county) <1pts>
CREATE INDEX covid_state_county_idx ON covid (state, county);

-- CREATE INDEX
#TODO [then run the same EXPLAIN ANALYZE again. <1pts>]
-- Bitmap Heap Scan on covid
-- Bitmap Index Scan on covid_state_county_idx
-- Execution Time: 1.168 ms
#TODO [Use a query to determine the size of the table alone, of its indexes alone and of both together <1pts>]
SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_table_size('covid')) AS table_size,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_indexes_size('covid')) AS index_size,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size('covid')) AS total;

-- table_size | index_size | total
-- 57 MB      | 6344 kB    | 63 MB
```
#TODO [After the index was created, what is the new scan type and the execution time? <1pts>]
PostgreSQL used a Bitmap Index Scan on covid_state_county_idx, followed by a Bitmap Heap Scan on covid. The execution time was 1.168 ms.
